To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the waist-to-height ratio and weight-to-height power ratio are better measures of body fatness than BMI, and 2) BMI over-adjusts more for height than the waist-to-height or weight-to-height power ratios, and therefore is more likely to misestimate nutritional state.
the waist-to-height ratio has a lower residual correlation with height than does body mass index and is thus a better index of body fatness than is BMI.
the waist-to-height ratio has greater validity than BMI as a single measure of body fat and that the ratio is better related than BMI to chronic disease risk.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of simple anthropometric measures to estimate nutritional status and body fatness.
the relationship between the anthropometric measures of body size, and their use as indicators of nutritional status.
the use of anthropometric measures to predict chronic disease risk and outcomes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
BMI is a better predictor of disease risk than wtHR, but that wtHR is a better predictor than BMI.
BMI and wtHR are both misadjusted relative to weight/height p and waist/height p but that wtHR is usually better adjusted than BMI.
BMI is a less accurate measure of body fat content than wtHR, and is also more likely to misestimate nutritional state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
wtHR is usually better related (in the sense of having less residual correlation with height) to chronic disease markers and risk, morbidity and mortality than BMI.
wtHR is usually better than BMI as a simple anthropometic indicator of nutritional state.
the wtHR is a better measure of nutritional state for relating to chronic disease markers and outcome than BMI, but that it is still not perfect.
The main takeaway from our work is that
BMI is a poor anthropometric measure of nutritional state, especially when used in the same way as wtHR, and that the latter is preferable.
the waist-to-height ratio may be more useful than the body mass index in the clinical setting, especially when the goal is to assess the risk of chronic diseases.
wtHR has a smaller residual correlation with height than BMI, and is thus less likely to over- or underestimate body fatness.
